content.comment:
I have a few questions, and some comments about your paper.
Firstly, it is interesting to note that your model achieves similar performance with fewer parameters on MNIST and CIFAR-10. I think this is a step to addressing the large parameter-cost for capsule-layers. However, this aside, I have a few doubts.

1. A central part of capsule-networks is the concept of routing. While it is not necessary to use iterative mechanisms like dynamic routing to build deeper capsules from shallower ones, I believe that the original idea was to have a mechanism to capture consensus among shallower capsules. This is primarily to ensure that spatial relationships among capsules are learnt and used in detecting objects so that a neural network does not act by a detection-by-part mechanism. Your paper argues that such a procedure is not necessary, and instead has the routing coefficients to be learnable. 
   In the light of learning such object-relationships, I do not see much difference between non capsule-based models and your proposed method. Further, as consensus among predicting capsules can be determined by non-iterative methods I do not see why such methods be replaced by not having routing at all.

2. Given the role of routing in capsule networks, as more than curve-fitting for performance, and rather for better, more semantically accurate representations, I am unclear whether an evaluation on MNIST and CIFAR-10 are enough to justify the lack of routing.  

3. You have visualised convolutional layers and compared them against the capsule layers of your model. Is it possible to do such a study comparing capsule-layers instead?

Thank you for sharing your research. It has given me some insight into capsule networks
content.title: Few questions and comments

replying_to: Replying to Few questions and comments

content.comment:
Hi Sairaam, 

Thanks for the comment. We believe that the core of CapsNets are the 'capsules' which package a group of neurons as a whole. At each step, a capsule layer maps a tensor into a tensor while a convolutional layer maps a tensor into a scalar. The routing procedures, if heuristic, are not part of the optimization process, thus can not guarantee that the learned coupling coefficients are optimal for an objective function. This is not our guess, one recent work [1] has shown that dynamic routing, EM routing, as well as three other routing procedures, sometimes perform worse than random or uniform routing.  I really like the idea of routing given its semantically explainable attribute, but given the proof of our work as well as [1], routing procedures might not be necessary for CapsNets. I am not sure if this is enough, but I doubt that any heuristic routing solution would generalize well. 

As for visualizing the capsules, our primary purpose is to point out that CapsNets should have a different initialization method than those used for CNNs.  Thus we only compare the P-CapsNets with CNNs. 


[1] Capsule Networks Need an Improved Routing Algorithm

content.comment:
Dear Authors,
it is interesting to note that routing and random weight assignments give comparable results on classification performance for capsnet. I have read the paper you referenced, and guessed that it would have been of some influence in your work. 
  I would say that while encapsulating neurons into a  single vector-activation is a big feature of capsule networks, equivariance and learning spatial relationships are at the core. As I understand from the paper "Transforming Autoencoders" -  the first paper on capsule networks - vector-activations are a means to an end - that being a model which is spatially-aware in its representations. Consensus-based routing comes naturally from the use of vector-activations, as it is easy to compare vectors.
In other words, I would state that routing is more for representational expressivity than only for accuracy scores. This is the reason why I am not sure if random weight assignments are enough to guarantee good representations - fitting to get decent accuracies is relatively easier for neural networks.
  Thus, my main point is that only testing on classification tasks for MNIST and CIFAR-10 may not be enough to justify the absence of routing. I would hope for better experiments.
content.title: Still certain lingering doubts

replying_to: Replying to Still certain lingering doubts

content.comment:
Hi Sairaam, 

Thanks for the insightful comment. I agree with you on the evidence part. Although there exists some evidence that some heuristic routing procedures might not be necessary (our work) or potentially harmful [1], they are all based on a couple of classification tasks. It would be overstated to say that CapsNets do not need routing procedures. Further experiments on some complex tasks are necessary. The problem is that CaspNets with varied routing procedures, so far, haven't been found efficiently in extracting spatially-aware representations for complex tasks on large datasets, either. For example, it is still unknown whether we can build a 100-layer CaspNets (with or without routing procedures) that achieves better segmentation accuracy than Resnets on COCO with significantly fewer parameters. The biggest motivation for this work is to improve the scalability of CaspNets so it can be applied to some complex tasks on large datasets easier. 

I don't think that "random weight assignments are enough to guarantee good representations". I also doubt that current routing procedures generalize better than random or uniform weight assignments given the negative evidence in [1]. That's why we propose P-Caspents because learning the part-whole spatial relationship implicitly may be a better idea. 


[1] Capsule Networks Need an Improved Routing Algorithm

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Authors argue that the routing mechanism is unnecessary in a capsnet and one can just simply aggregate. They scale the matrix product introduced in Hinton 2018 to rank 3 tensors to decrease the number of parameters. Furthermore, they eliminate the free-form initial convolution layers.

The motivational derivation on equation 3 is simply wrong. c_ij is not a scalar or a learnt parameter. It is a function of c_ik at previous iteration for all other k. equation 3 would have been correct for a scalar or a learnt parameter but not a function of other parameters that just multiplication with W will not bring into the equation. Removing c_ij all together reduces capsule networks into simple CNNs, because there is no notion of agreement (cluster finding, attention) anymore. It is just a CNN with more weight sharing now. Also arguing that since number of parameters involved is jut 7 percent it is not important is just nonsense. The importance of a parameter is not based on the quantity. Several routing iterations may indeed be unnecessary, but a grouping mechanism need to still validate if the votes agree or not or it will be simple pattern matching like normal CNNs. 

CapsNets where proposed as a network that have comparable classification accuracy with CNNs with the extra benefit of the transformation generalization. If the classification accuracy was the primary goal one would have just used ResNets or etc. There is complete ignorance to the main point of CapsNets (viewpoint generalization) throughout the paper. No experiments showing any viewpoint generalizability of the current proposed network. 

As for Adversarial Robustness of EMCapsNet, they also have fewer parameters incompare to the baseline CNN. I would argue the white box rebustness exactly comes from the aggregation method (here essentially an xor function is replaced with addition).

replying_to: Replying to Official Blind Review #2
display_title: The reviewer seems to misunderstand the idea

content.title: The reviewer seems to misunderstand the idea
content.comment:
Thanks for the comment. 

1. c_ij can be considered as a learned parameter. Please check Hinton's latest paper, "stacked capsule encoders". There is no routing and the c_ij is learned explicitly.  Similar evidence can be found in paper "capsule networks with trainable routing procedures" as well as this paper. 

2. The reviewer's comment "Removing c_ij all together reduces capsule networks into simple CNNs" is incorrect. Capsule layers are more general versions of convolutional layers, please check Figure 1 for details. 

3. The reviewer seems to believe that the primary purpose of this paper is about the accuracy of classification ("If the classification accuracy was the primary goal one would have just used ResNets or etc."). But our purpose is about efficiency rather than accuracy. 

4. I am not sure if the reviewer is right about the reason for the robustness of CapsNets (I believe that the robustness comes from the randomness introduced by the heuristic routing procedure). I agree with the reviewer that EMCaspNets model is also small, (4.2M CNN VS 310K CapsNet),  but our model is even smaller (8M CNN versus 4K CaspNet)

In conclusion, the reviews seem to believe that the core of CaspNets is the routing procedure, but we believe that the core is "grouping neurons into capsules" and the coupling coefficients can be learned and optimized (and thus the routing procedure is not necessary).

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes to improve the Capsule Networks by making three empirical modifications to them:
1. Without using routing procedure from CapsNets
2. Without using convolutional layers
3. Using higher-rank tensors to save parameters

With these modifications, they achieve comparable performance with much fewer parameters. In the experiments, they also show some interesting insight on the initialization of CapsNets. Overall, this paper is well written, easy to understand. However, I have the following concerns:

1. The P-CapsNet outperforms the original one. Which one of the three modification contributes the most to the improvement? A comprehensive ablation study should be done in this work.

2. The P-CapsNets shows competitive without requiring the expensive routing procedure. However, the generalization ability is not the only way to evaluate capsule networks. It is not clear whether other properties of CapsNets are affected by the removal of the routing procedure.

3. In P-CapsNets, the basic unit of input, output, and capsules are all rank-3 tensors. The Equation 4 is obtained by extending Equation 3 to the 3D case and incorporating the convolution operation. What is the relationship between this work can DeepCaps[1] where they apply 3D convolution based dynamic routing algorithm?

[1] Rajasegaran, Jathushan, et al. "DeepCaps: Going Deeper with Capsule Networks." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

4. In Section 7, the adversarial robustness of CapsNets is evaluated. The paper claims that P-CapsNets also suffer this issue, even more seriously than CNN models. Do the experiments with the Basic Iterative Method (BIM) show the same result? The experiment should be done as in Hinton et al. (2018).

5. The universal adversary perturbation (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. (2016)) is applied to evaluate the resistance to white-box attack. Why this work chooses this one instead of a popular white-box attack method (e.g., FGSM as in Hinton et al. (2018))?

replying_to: Replying to Official Blind Review #3

content.title: Thanks for the comment!
content.comment:
Thanks for the comment! Below is my reply to your concerns:

1. All three modifications are designed to improve efficiency. Specifically, replacing convolutional layers with capsule layers can reduce the number of parameters significantly which is obvious. Packing neurons into high-rank tensors also save parameters, please check the examples in our paper. Removing the expensive routing procedures can save running time in both training and testing time. The efficiency can be improved by our designs is straight-forward so we thought it might not be necessary to do the ablation analysis. 

2. The unnecessity of a heuristic routing procedure can be proved both mathematically and experimentally, as shown in our paper that our model can achieve better performance by using significantly fewer parameters. Besides, Hinton's recent paper "stacked capsule autoencoders" also removes heuristic routing procedures and acquires the coupling coefficients by learning. You can also find some evidence in "Capsule Networks Need an Improved Routing Algorithm"

3. Our method is fundamentally different from DeepCaps, 1). we do not use any type of routing procedures explicitly; 2). We consider a capsule layer as a mapping between tensors and tensors while a convolutional layer(including 1D, 2D, 3D convolution)  a mapping between tensors and scalars.

4&5.  We just want to provide more evidence for the conclusion that "CapsNets also suffer for white-box attack". You need only one negative evidence to disprove the conclusion that "Capsnets are more robust to black-box adversarial attacking".

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper presents a new architecture that takes inspiration from capsule networks and CNNs. Specifically the authors propose a layer called the capsule layer which takes a rank 3 tensor as input and outputs another rank 3 tensor. 

The authors also discuss routing procedures but ultimately there proposal does not have any routing procedure, and their architecture can be thought in a more straightforward manner as a generalization of a CNN. The fundamenta lconjecture in the paper is that " the strong modeling ability of CapsNets come from this tensor to tensor mapping between adjacent capsule layers" and the authors demonstrate this empirically on CIFAR and MNIST dataset.

The basic way in which the authors generalize CNNs is by using elementwise-multiplication and addition between 3D tensors to create an algebra (strictly speaking a ring, but nothing stops the authors from using elementwise division as well) over these elements. After this step the 3D tensors can be treated simply as scalars. In essence this ties the weights that can act on each 3D tensor and results in parameter reduction. 


The strong point of the paper is the great empirical performance of the proposed neural network architecture on the CIFAR and MNIST datasets. Unfortunately, it seems to me that this is not nearly enough work to conclusively show the importance/utility of this idea. There are many other datasets/benchmarks such as Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-100, and larger datasets such as ImageNet that are now considered essential for acceptance of a purely empirical contribution such as a new neural network architecture.  

Because of the above reasons I cannot recommend acceptance of the paper in its current state.

replying_to: Replying to Official Blind Review #1
display_title: Thanks for the comment, but seems like you misunderstand the idea

content.title: Thanks for the comment, but seems like you misunderstand the idea
content.comment:
Thanks for the comment! 

First, the basic operation of P-CapsNets is not "elementwise-multiplication and addition", but a tensor product. 

Second, "After this step the 3D tensors can be treated simply as scalars. " is also incorrect, we adopt rank-3 tensors as basic units all along with the network. 

Third, the primary contribution of our paper is to propose a scalable version of CapsNet,  thus we focus on this new structure of neural networks as the first step. It is true that this structure should be further tested in large datasets, we are doing that and planing to publish another paper.
